content: The receptor activator of nuclear factor κB (RANK), also referred to as the TNFRSF11A or TRANCE receptor, is a member of the tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) molecular sub-family. RANK serves as the receptor for RANK-Ligand (RANKL) and is a critical component of the RANK/RANKL/OPG signaling pathway, which governs the differentiation and activation of osteoclasts. This pathway is essential for processes such as bone remodeling and repair, immune cell function, lymph node development, thermoregulation, and mammary gland development. Osteoprotegerin (OPG) acts as a decoy receptor for RANK, modulating the RANK signaling pathway by competing with RANKL. The cytoplasmic domain of RANK interacts with TRAF proteins (TRAF1, TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6), which transmit signals to downstream targets like NF-κB and JNK. RANK is constitutively expressed in various tissues, including skeletal muscle, thymus, liver, colon, small intestine, adrenal gland, osteoclasts, mammary gland epithelial cells, prostate, vascular cells, and pancreas. While RANKL is the primary mediator of NF-κB activation, overexpression of RANK alone can also activate the NF-κB pathway. RANKL is expressed on the surface of stromal cells, osteoblasts, and T cells. Structurally, RANK is a type I transmembrane protein composed of 616 amino acids. Its extracellular domain contains 184 amino acids, the transmembrane domain has 21 amino acids, and the cytoplasmic domain consists of 383 amino acids. Like other members of the TNFR family, RANK has four extracellular cysteine-rich pseudo-repeat domains (CRDs). It shares 40% amino acid identity with CD40 and exhibits 85% homology between mouse and human homologues. RANK exists as two monomers related by noncrystallographic two-fold symmetry perpendicular to the long axis of the molecules. The four CRDs span a length of 100 angstroms, making RANK the longest member of the TNFR family identified to date. Binding of RANKL to RANK induces receptor trimerization and activates downstream signaling pathways. The RANK-RANKL complex forms a heterohexameric structure, with only two of the four RANK CRDs directly interacting with RANKL. Most residues in the complex are hydrophilic, and unlike other TNFSF members, the surface interactions in the RANK-RANKL complex are continuous. In osteoclastogenesis, TRAF6 is indispensable for the RANK-mediated pathway. RANKL binds to RANK, which subsequently recruits TRAF6. TRAF6 activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathways, leading to osteoclast differentiation and activation. This system is tightly regulated by the relative expression of OPG and RANKL, which are influenced by hormones, immune signals, and growth factors. Overexpression of RANKL can result in excessive osteoclast production and activation, leading to bone resorption. The balance between RANKL and OPG is a therapeutic target for conditions such as estrogen deficiency-associated osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Paget’s disease, periodontal disease, and bone tumors or malignancies. RANK also plays a pivotal role in thermoregulation, particularly in females, where it is regulated by ovarian sex hormones. RANK is expressed in key brain regions involved in thermoregulation. Inactivation of RANK in these areas abolishes the fever response to elevated RANKL levels. RANK is also a critical mediator of fever responses induced by lipopolysaccharides and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and TNFα. This role of the RANK-RANKL system may explain the link between osteoporosis and hot flashes observed in postmenopausal women. In mammary gland development, RANK is constitutively expressed in mammary epithelial tissues. Calcium transfer from mother to fetus and neonate is facilitated by increased osteoclastic activity, which is regulated by the RANK/RANKL axis. RANKL also signals through RANK to promote the proliferation and survival of cells during the final stages of lactating mammary gland development. Dysfunctional RANK or RANKL impairs the differentiation and expansion of alveolar buds into mature lobulo-alveolar structures, thereby inhibiting milk production. Clinically, RANK and RANKL are implicated in certain cancers, including breast and prostate cancers. RANKL expression in infiltrating T cells within mammary carcinomas activates RANK-expressing neoplastic mammary epithelial cells, promoting metastasis. The expression of RANKL in these cells and RANK in bone cells may represent the biological basis of Paget’s seed and soil hypothesis. The affinity of RANKL for RANK may explain the propensity of these cancers to metastasize to bone. Once tumors are established in bone, they stimulate bone resorption by secreting factors like RANKL or inducing surrounding stromal cells to express growth factors. These growth factors upregulate RANKL production, leading to osteoclastogenesis and bone destruction. This bone destruction releases additional growth factors and RANKL, perpetuating a vicious cycle of bone degradation observed in metastatic bone tumors. Therapeutically, most interventions targeting the RANK/RANKL/OPG axis aim to downregulate RANKL expression or upregulate OPG expression. For instance, denosumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody against RANKL, has been shown in phase I and II trials to reduce bone resorption in patients with multiple myeloma, prostate cancer, and breast cancer. Other studies have explored the development of small mimetics based on OPG’s structure that bind to both RANK and RANKL, disrupting their interaction. RANK has been shown to interact with TRAF1, TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6, which are critical mediators of its downstream signaling pathways.
